comments.author: spc476
comments.text:
As I read this, I was reminded of two quotes.  The first is about the taste gap from Ira Glass:


Nobody tells this to people who are beginners, I wish someone told me. All of us who do creative work, we get into it because we have good taste. But there is this gap. For the first couple years you make stuff, it’s just not that good. It’s trying to be good, it has potential, but it’s not. But your taste, the thing that got you into the game, is still killer. And your taste is why your work disappoints you. A lot of people never get past this phase, they quit. Most people I know who do interesting, creative work went through years of this. We know our work doesn’t have this special thing that we want it to have. We all go through this. And if you are just starting out or you are still in this phase, you gotta know its normal and the most important thing you can do is do a lot of work. Put yourself on a deadline so that every week you will finish one story. It is only by going through a volume of work that you will close that gap, and your work will be as good as your ambitions. And I took longer to figure out how to do this than anyone I’ve ever met. It’s gonna take awhile. It’s normal to take awhile. You’ve just gotta fight your way through.


The second is from The Ze Frank Show:


For a very long time, taste and artistic training have been things that only a small number of people have been able to develop. Only a few people could afford to participate in the production of many types of media. Raw materials like pigments were expensive; same with tools like printing presses; even as late as 1963 it cost Charles Peignot over $600,000 to create and cut a single font family.

The small number of people who had access to these tools and resources created rules about what was good taste or bad taste. These designers started giving each other awards and the rules they followed became even more specific. All sorts of stuff about grids and sizes and color combinations — lots of stuff that the consumers of this media never consciously noticed. Over the last 20 years, however, the cost of tools related to the authorship of media has plummeted. For very little money, anyone can create and distribute things like newsletters, or videos, or bad-ass tunes about "ugly."

Suddenly consumers are learning the language of these authorship tools. The fact that tons of people know names of fonts like Helvetica is weird! And when people start learning something new, they perceive the world around them differently. If you start learning how to play the guitar, suddenly the guitar stands out in all the music you listen to. For example, throughout most of the history of movies, the audience didn't really understand what a craft editing was. Now, as more and more people have access to things like iMovie, they begin to understand the manipulative power of editing. Watching reality TV almost becomes like a game as you try to second-guess how the editor is trying to manipulate you.

As people start learning and experimenting with these languages authorship, they don't necessarily follow the rules of good taste. This scares the shit out of designers.


I'm not sure what I make of all this.

comments.author: tombh
comments.text:
Everyone can make anything. Almost no one can tell you what is worth making.


Whilst I agree with the sentiment, it feels like quite a narrow view. I think it's possible to argue that in actual fact AI has taken very little from us. To paraphrase Graeber's Bullshit Jobs: AI mostly only amplifies pre-existing bullshitery. The signal is still there, just as loud and clear as ever, but the noise has changed, that's all.

It was always hard to find meaningful and fulfilling work, whether paid or personal. Maybe it felt like we had it a bit easier pre-AI, in the sense that yes, not everyone could make anything. Us geeks could do the monkey work and get well paid or receive open source kudos. But if that's all we ever contributed, then of course AI looks like a usurper.

Computers are hard for so many more reasons than the mere act of making things. Consider the humanity. I cannot express my gratitude for the warm smiles of colleagues on a dreary Monday morning, or the patient and considered comments from a stranger on a tricky Github Issue. Not only is that still left after AI, it hasn't even taken a dent.

Then there's the whole issue of copyright. Putting aside the legality of AI training, the morality of attributing our sources is still left after AI. I care about who makes my software. I value their time and wish for them to be recognised for their efforts. AI doesn't stop me having or expressing those feelings.

And of course the environmental impact of data centres. The deepening of the socio-political capitalistic violence of the concentration of wealth from AI investment. At the very least we still have the choice to be conscious of those things, and ideally we make a stand against them with our wallets and voices.

To say that taste is all that's left feels either superficial or like giving up. Keep your head up! If you value good, true work, if you care about other humans, if the craft inspires you, then it's all still up for grabs. In fact this is engineering: navigating unprecedented circumstances with patience, creativity and kindness. To state the hacker credo:


Do what you can, with what you have, where you are.

comments.author: shonfeder
comments.text:
The post references William Morris and John Ruskin thus:


Morris and Ruskin among them, looked at the flood of cheap identical goods and asked a question that sounded, at the time, sentimental and doomed: not can we make this, but should this be made, and made this way, by no one, for no reason but that the machine could.

They lost the economic argument. They were always going to. But they were right about the thing that mattered, which is that when the making becomes free, the choosing becomes the craft.


Read literally, this claims that Morris and Ruskin maintain a thesis like this: in the wake of the mechanization of production, "choosing becomes the craft".

I'm not versed in this movement or their writings, but I tried to look into this. Ruskin seemed to hold that engaging in healthy creative labour was essential to being a good person. From Stones of Venice Volume II, chapter VI, section 16. (According to crafts person Robin Wood):


It can only be met by a right understanding, on the part of all classes, of what kinds of labour are good for men, raising them, and making them happy; by a determined sacrifice of such convenience or beauty, or cheapness as is to be got only by the degradation of the workman; and by equally determined demand for the products and results of healthy and ennobling labour.


Morris wrote an essay, Useful Work versus Useless Toil critiquing the way mechanization was being misused to intensify toil:


They are called "labour-saving" machines - a commonly used phrase which implies what we expect of them; but we do not get what we expect. What they really do is to reduce the skilled labourer to the ranks of the unskilled, to increase the number of the "reserve army of labour" - that is, to increase the precariousness of life among the workers and to intensify the labour of those who serve the machines (as slaves their masters). All this they do by the way, while the pile up the profits of the employers of labour, or force them to expend those profits in bitter commercial war with each other. In a true society these miracles of ingenuity would be for the first time used for minimizing the amount of time spent in unattractive labour, which by their means might be so reduced as to be but a very light burden on each individual. All the more as these machines would most certainly be very much improved when it was no longer a question as to whether their improvement would "pay" the individual, but rather whether it would benefit the community.


Here's an encapsulation from a reputable source:


Ruskin and William Morris, looked to the artisan guilds of the Middle Ages for inspiration. The ethical and political dimensions of Ruskin’s The Nature of the Gothic, in particular, inspired Morris’s belief in art as the expression of man’s joy in labour. In Metcalf’s view, “Ruskin’s genius was to move attention away from a disinterested contemplation of an artwork and toward a broader examination of the society from which the work emerges” (“Contemporary” 16). Moreover, Ruskin’s version of the history of the Middle Ages strongly influenced Morris’s. In “Architecture and History,” Morris explains his belief that all workmen were artists in the Middle Ages and that this situation began to change in the sixteenth century, creating a division of labour between workmen and artists. By the late eighteenth century, this division had reduced workmen to machines. By the late nineteenth century, Morris felt that the situation was even worse; workmen were now slaves to machines. Morris believed a way to combat this problem was to change manufacturing conditions in order to reinstate the social relations of production of Middle Ages artisan guilds. In “The Revival of Handicraft,” Morris argues that


we do sorely need a system of production which will give us beautiful surroundings and pleasant occupation, and which will tend to make us good human animals, able to do something for ourselves, so that we may be generally intelligent. (https://utppublishing.com/doi/10.3138/CRAS.2014.S06)


Starting with the individual, human animal and then moving to the societal level, the Arts and Crafts movement sought to “reassert unity in a world perceived to be artificially fragmented,” according to historian Tom Crook (26). The ideal place of unity was the workshop, where social solidarity and the production of objects necessary for life combined.


I notice these themes in the snippets I've found on the Arts and Crafts Movement:


the unity of thought and labour

the inseparable relation between social conditions and means of production

the basic tension between the organisation of labour and the distribution of capital

the way that the artistry of human judgment and the practice of laborious creation are mutually constituting


Which seem virtually anathema to the view presented in this post. Curious that it was named as a central point of reference!

comments.text:
I'm sorry, but I just struggle accepting your claim. And to explain the reactions you're getting, it's like this: imagine that someone rings your doorbell 100 times and every time, you find flaming poo on your doorstep. You're not going to give it the benefit of the doubt when the doorbell rings for the 101th time, right?

Here's what immediately makes me very skeptical about your claim: (1) I can't find your pre-LLM writing that would be comparable in style or verbosity; (2) I see a wide number of consistent, high-level tells in the text (and I don't mean em-dashes); (3) your essay scores 100% AI on Pangram, which is a remarkably good tool (in contrast to the crappy detectors of the old); (4) your essay doesn't seem to be saying anything beyond what I'd expect an LLM to produce in response to a short prompt - the "thesis compression" test.

I'll admit that my judgment is colored by the fact that it's a peculiar affliction of AI-related op-eds (both pro- and con-) that they appear to be AI-generated at a much higher rate than any other form of blogging on the internet. Their authors often show up to assert that they haven't used AI tools, but in almost all instances, these claims are difficult to take seriously. I remember debating someone who had no online writing footprint whatsoever until 2025 and then started a blog that posted one long-form piece every single day at the same hour. Is there a one-in-a-million chance I was talking to a pseudonymous programming blog prodigy who works on a really precise schedule? Yes, but you gotta draw the line somewhere.

And it matters to me because if I'm to spend human time reading, reflecting on, and engaging with a post, I want to engage with content where another human actually put in the effort to articulate their own thoughts. I don't want to engage with an endless supply of machine-generated posts. There's just no point.

On the off chance you're actually being honest with us - it sucks, but I think you should direct your ire toward the flaming-poo pranksters who came before.

comments.author: notashelf
comments.text:
There is not much I can add from this point forward, but I hear and understand your concerns, to say the least. Do consider my perspective, though: I'm an anonymous hobbyist doing this for the hell of it. The blog, the software I write, and anything else I have produced provides more value to the consumer than it does to me. It is not my day job, and it will never benefit me in my day job. Even if the post gets 100,000 reads, the value it provides to me is little to none. I do appreciate you taking the time to comment---and taking the time to honestly criticize even more so. If you like consuming human content, I like producing it. If I were to have a LLM produce a post for me and throw it out there, I would only be shooting myself in the foot. Great, now I have made myself obsolete.

I'm trying to be honest with you---all of you who took the time to comment---because I do appreciate the criticism. Even a "this sucks, Claude wrote this" is valuable feedback that I am taking to heart. But even if I decide now that yes, the post must be rewritten because it sounds too much like AI, there is nothing else I can do. My writing style is my writing style. Everything since 2025---and the sloppier, worse-edited stuff that shortly predates it---is what I can produce. Again, I can only apologize for having you doubt the authenticity of the post, and only that.

The doorbell analogy is fair. I do not mean to pretend I am owed the benefit of the doubt when I am the 101st ring, and I can't really argue my way out of a detector score and I'm not going to try. If the tells are there, they're there. What I will do, however, is to take the criticism and advice into heart. I harbor no ire towards you and no negative or skeptic-at-best comment for expecting the worst. It is what is. I apologized, and I said my piece.

comments.author: shonfeder
comments.text:
I also found this an incredible claim given the content and style of the writing. It's interesting that the piece itself takes the position that the way things are produced ultimately doesn't matter, and only judgment matters


the judgement itself. The part that was always the point.


Yet the author seems to be at pains to convince incredulous readers that this was not machine generated. An interesting tension there!

Regardless of the actual provenance in this case, I think the proliferation of LLMs are supercharging a process of homogenizing of language and thinking that has been going on for a long time. The best encapsulation of this I've found so far is in Adorno's "Prisms" (from 1967):


The notion of the free expression of opinion, indeed, that of intellectual freedom itself in bourgeois society, upon which cultural criticism is founded, has its own dialectic. For while the mind extricated itself from a theological-feudal tutelage, it has fallen increasingly under the anonymous sway of the status quo. This regimentation, the result of the progressive societalization of all human relations, did not simply confront the mind from without; it immigrated into its immanent consistency. It imposes itself as relentlessly on the autonomous mind as heteronomous orders were formerly imposed on the mind which was bound. Not only does the mind mold itself for the sake of its marketability, and thus reproduce socially prevalent categories. Rather, it grows to resemble ever more closely the status quo even where it subjectively refrains from making a commodity of itself. The network of the whole is drawn every tighter, modeled after the act of exchange. It leaves the individual consciousness less and less room for evasion, preforms it more and more thoroughly, cuts it off a priori as it were from the possibility of differencing itself as all difference degenerates to a nuance in the monotony of supply.   (Adorno 1981, "Prisms")

comments.author: mtset
comments.text:
After reading this reply, I read the addendum, and then read a few of your other posts. I will say that many others very much do not sound like slop; when I compare them using the various AI detectors [1], posts from early 2025 say 10% or 0% and newer ones, including this one, say 100% AI or "AI paraphrased." That shift seems to have taken place, to my eye and to those of the detectors, between "The Federation Fallacy" (June 26, 2025) and "The Tradeoff Trap" (August 10, 2025).

I'm really torn: on the one hand, you seem very genuine, and I'd really like to believe that there were no LLMs involved. On the other hand, there are just so many of these tells present, from jarringly different sentences composed of three or four words in the form "<noun> <verb> [article] <noun>" to the little thinking-outside-of-thinking phrases like "I want to be careful here", "Here is the uncomfortable mechanism", and "[H]ere is the defense, such as it is" that emerge from the mechanism of LLMs' relentless forward march of token completion, that it's hard for me to believe.

If it's really true that the machines write like you, I'm sorry. That's awful. With that said, I do think that writing well these days means taking the time to make clear, through both careful editing and clear sentence construction, that what we put out doesn't sound like the machine -- and I wonder what happened about a year ago that made you stop doing that.

1: To me, the comparison is much more interesting than the raw number. I understand that simply reporting "GPTZero says AI" is mostly meaningless.

That shift seems to have taken place, to my eye and to those of the detectors, between "The Federation Fallacy" (June 26, 2025) and "The Tradeoff Trap" (August 10, 2025).


AI detector or not, I have been feeling the same drop in quality and insight in my posts and I, well, can't pretend there hasn't been a shift. I'd be lying to you and to myself if I had said I didn't see it. Consequently, I have re-read my post after it hit Hacker News and a friend kindly informing me of it. I'll tell you this much: the only thing I had in my mind was "how the FUCK did I write like this". Hilariously, I was thinking "I have not written anything with real depth in a while" to myself earlier this week.


If it's really true that the machines write like you, I'm sorry. That's awful. With that said, I do think that writing well these days means taking the time to make clear, through both careful editing and clear sentence construction, that what we put out doesn't sound like the machine -- and I wonder what happened about a year ago that made you stop doing that.


I have spent a good while contemplating whether it was the machines that write like me, or if I write like the machines. I hesitate to say I think it is a combination of both. What I did do---without ever clocking it as a decision---was spend a year reading the things and working next to them daily, until their "cadence" was part of my mental archive.

Again, I appreciate your comment. I wrote the post with good, albeit selfish, intentions but it was never the goal to drop unfiltered LLM slop in the timeline and wait for clout. That goes against all the reasons I write. Admittedly I am embarrassed to have produced such a piece. Now that I think about it, I've read enough of the averaged voice that some of it has settled into mine, and the tells you can name are ones I reach for practically unprompted now---like the way you pick up an accent without deciding to. Yes I mentally filter out the typical tells like "This isn't X, this is Y" and the many like it, but clearly some have made it into my lexicon.

Like many comments such as yours, the care and the concern have been a wake-up call. I started working on a second post---partially inspired by this one---and if you ever get around to reading it then I leave it to you whether it reads as mine or as the machine's. With all of those said, I can't help but read my own writing with a certain level of paranoia after the fact. Much I should think about. Still, I leave you with my thanks.
